title: Exercise race horses at various paces on a sand track

lessons.title: Before going onto the sand track
lessons.html:
The work rider's job

Racehorses are exercised every day to build fitness. Work riders ride them on the training track at the paces and distances the trainer sets. On many South African training centres this is a sand track. The work rider must follow instructions exactly, because the trainer plans each horse's work carefully to bring it to peak fitness without injury.

Getting instructions

Before each lot goes out, check the work board or ask the trainer:

  • Which horse you ride
  • Which track and which direction
  • What paces and distances: for example walk, trot, canter, then a faster piece of work
  • Whether you work alone or alongside another horse ("in company")
  • Any special notes: the horse pulls, shies, or must be kept on the inside

If you do not understand, ask. Never guess.

Protective equipment

  • A certified skull cap (helmet), done up
  • A body protector (safety vest)
  • Boots with a heel, and gloves
  • Goggles where sand is kicked back

Checking the horse and tack

  1. Check the girth and surcingle are tight and the saddle is in place.
  2. Check the bridle, bit, reins and any special gear.
  3. Adjust your stirrups to the length you need for the work.
  4. Look for any sign of lameness as the horse walks out of the yard. Report it to the trainer before the horse works.

Track rules

Every training track has rules set by the training centre. Common ones are:

  • Enter and leave the track only at marked gates.
  • Walk and trot on the outside; faster work on the inside, or as the centre rules state.
  • Keep to the set direction of travel.
  • Never stop or turn suddenly on the track.
  • Look and listen before crossing or entering.
  • Follow the instructions of track officials.

lessons.title: Riding the paces and finishing the work
lessons.html:
Paces on the track

PacePurposeRider
WalkWarm up and cool downRelaxed, long rein but in control
TrotLoosen musclesRising trot or standing in short stirrups
Canter (slow work)Build staminaTwo-point position, steady even rhythm
Faster work (half-speed, gallop work as instructed)Build speed and fitnessShorter stirrups, balanced over the withers, steady contact

Controlling the pace

The trainer often gives the work as distances and a speed, for example "canter 1 600 m steady, then 600 m half-speed". Use the furlong markers or distance poles to know where you are. Keep an even rhythm; do not let the horse pull you faster than instructed. A horse that goes too fast in work can get tired, injured or "leave its race on the track".

Using the bridge

Work riders often hold the reins in a bridge: the reins crossed over the horse's neck so that both hands hold both reins, giving a stable support. Press the bridge onto the neck to steady a horse that pulls. Do not jerk the mouth.

Working in company

When two horses work together, keep the distance the trainer wants: upsides (side by side) or a set length behind. Talk to the other rider. Do not cut across in front of another horse.

Pulling up

  1. At the end of the work, look behind before you move off the line.
  2. Pull up gradually over a long distance, not suddenly.
  3. Move to the outside rail as the track rules state.
  4. Walk until the horse's breathing settles.

After the work

Report to the trainer: how the horse went, whether it blew hard, pulled, changed legs, hung to one side, or felt uneven. This information helps the trainer plan. Check the legs after the horse is washed down.

Emergencies

If a horse goes lame on the track, pull up safely and get off if needed. If you fall, stay down and keep your arms over your head until loose horses have passed, unless you are in danger. Report every incident.

Key points

  • Get exact instructions on horse, track, paces and distances before you ride.
  • Always wear a skull cap and body protector.
  • Follow track rules: marked gates, direction, no sudden stops.
  • Use distance markers and keep an even rhythm at the set pace.
  • Pull up gradually and report how the horse went to the trainer.
